newsitem.title: UK: Dlr rangebound in Europe as payrolls vigil begins.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rangebound in Europe as payrolls vigil begins.

text.p: The dollar was mildly softer across the board in early Europe, but analysts saw little cause for alarm and predicted a day of quiet range-trading as the market awaited Friday's U.S. payrolls and German jobless data.
Lingering concerns over European monetary union and Germany's budget problems, plus the prospect of a strong U.S. payrolls report, were seen underpinning dollar/mark.

Dollar/yen, however, was weighed down by news of a healthy Japanese trade surplus in the first 20 days of May and comments from the Bank of Japan governor which rekindled speculation of monetary tightening there.
Japan posted a 41.16 billion yen surplus for the first 20 days of last month, compared with a 180.94 billion deficit in the same period last year.

"The trade surplus is still going up and will continue to go up. That's the strongest factor supporting the yen, but also the view that Japanese rates are going up at some stage is going to return to the market," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.
The rate-hike fever which swept the market last month has cooled lately. But BOJ governor Yasuo Matsushita said overnight the bank was ready to act pre-emptively on monetary policy.
The dollar was quoted at 115.89/99 yen at 0801 GMT, down from late Wednesday's European level of 116.22/32, and at 1.7254/59 marks versus 1.7308/13.
Dealers said dollar/mark's downside attempts reflected market frustration rather than true bearishness.

"The market's a bit fed up with trying to take the dollar higher, so we'll have a look at the downside and see if there are any stops around," said Nick Probert, head of spot trading at Bank of America here.
The U.S. currency should find decent support around 1.7220 marks, Probert said.
But the broader picture is a supportive one for dollar/mark.
"Lingering uncertainty about EMU and a strong U.S. employment report should give the dollar strength against the deutschemark," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London.

Though the row between the German government and Bundesbank over Bonn's asset revaluation plans has been settled, analysts said real concerns remain over the whole EMU project and the prospect of a broad-based, weak euro.
Germany's difficulty in plugging its budget holes and France's new left-wing government are part of that uncertainty.

On the U.S. side of the coin, the May non-farm payrolls report will be crucial as the market scouts for clues on whether the Federal Reserve will tighten policy next month. A strong payrolls number is therefore seen refuelling the dollar.
"The payrolls will almost set the tone for the next month's trading in terms of the market's U.S. interest rate expectations," said Coleman at CIBC.

Although seasonal revisions from the U.S. Labor Department have prompted many economists to lower their forecasts, a Reuter poll still shows average expectations of a 219,000 rise in May payrolls compared to April's 142,000 increase.

German unemployment data for May are also due out on Friday. Thursday's Berliner Zeitung newspaper, citing the Federal Labour Office, said seasonally-adjusted jobless rose 60,000 in May but fell by around 90,000 to 4.25 million on an unadjusted basis.
Data out early Thursday showed pan-German first-quarter GDP rose 0.5 percent on the quarter and 1.4 year-on-year versus expected increases of 0.3 and 2.6 percent respectively.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the latest data could have a beneficial impact on the country's deficit, but said they were not yet impacting the labour market.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
